title: Sum Over Subsets (SOS DP)
directAnswer: For every mask, you want F[mask] = sum of A[s] over all submasks s of mask. Enumerating submasks directly is O(3ⁿ). Sum Over Subsets DP does it in O(2ⁿ · n): process one bit i at a time, and for every mask that has bit i set, add in F[mask without bit i]. After all n bits, each F[mask] holds the full subset sum. It's a dimension-by-dimension prefix sum over the Boolean hypercube.

remember.pattern: SOS DP — accumulate one bit dimension at a time over the hypercube
rules: Initialize `F = A` (each mask starts holding only its own value).
Outer loop over **bits** i, inner loop over **masks** — never swap the nesting.
Only update masks where bit i is set; add the value of the mask with bit i cleared.
After bit i, `F[mask]` holds the sum over submasks that may differ from `mask` only in bits `0..i`.
It's a 2ⁿ × n in-place DP; for **superset** sums flip the update to `F[mask without bit i] += F[mask]`.
whenToUse: You need subset-sum (or subset-aggregate) for every mask at once
Counting pairs / triples by subset or superset containment over bitmasks
Convolutions over the subset lattice (AND/OR convolution building blocks)
Replacing an O(3ⁿ) submask loop with O(2ⁿ · n)
antiSignals: You need only one mask's subset sum → a single O(2^popcount) submask walk is enough
n is large (≥ ~22) → 2ⁿ memory is infeasible regardless
The aggregate isn't decomposable bit-by-bit (e.g. depends on order) → SOS doesn't apply
Plain prefix sums on an array → standard 1-D prefix, not hypercube DP
remember.takeaway: SOS DP is a multidimensional prefix sum on the n-bit hypercube: relax one bit at a time and each mask absorbs its submasks in O(2ⁿ · n). Once you see subsets as points in a Boolean cube, the bit-by-bit relaxation is just prefix-summing along each axis.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can turn an O(3ⁿ) submask enumeration into O(2ⁿ · n) by recognizing subset-sum as a prefix sum along each bit dimension, and order the loops correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Swapping the loop nesting (masks outside, bits inside) or double-counting by reading already-updated entries, both of which corrupt the dimension-by-dimension invariant.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Frame SOS as a hypercube prefix sum, state the per-bit invariant precisely, and contrast it with the naive O(3ⁿ) submask loop.

problemStatement:
You are given an integer `n` and an array `A` of length `2ⁿ`, where `A[s]` is a value associated with the bitmask `s` (a subset of an n-element ground set).

For every mask `m` in `[0, 2ⁿ - 1]`, compute `F[m] = Σ A[s]` over **all submasks** `s` of `m` (every `s` with `s & m == s`).

Return the array `F`.
constraints: Values fit in a 64-bit integer (use long / Python int)
A submask s of m satisfies (s & m) == s; m is a submask of itself, and 0 is a submask of every m
understanding: Think of each mask as a vertex of an n-dimensional cube of 0/1 coordinates. F[m] sums A over every vertex 'below' m in the subset order (every submask). Doing this independently per mask is expensive; SOS DP shares work across masks by relaxing one coordinate axis at a time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a mask a submask of itself, and is 0 a submask of everything?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes to both. (s & m) == s includes s = m and s = 0, so F[m] always includes A[m] and A[0].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want subset sums or superset sums?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subset sums here (sum over s ⊆ m). The superset variant flips the update direction — worth mentioning.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I overwrite A in place, or must F be separate?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place is standard and saves memory; I'll copy A into F first to keep the input intact, but the DP itself is in place on F.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How big can n get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 20, so 2ⁿ ≈ 1,048,576 entries. O(2ⁿ · n) ≈ 21 million ops is fine; O(3ⁿ) would be ~3.5 billion and too slow.

examples.explanation: Only A[11] is nonzero; its only supermask is 11 itself, so just F[11]=1.

approaches.name: Naive Submask Enumeration
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to establish correctness and the O(3ⁿ) cost, then say 'we can share work across masks'.
hints: For a single mask m, how do you iterate exactly its submasks without touching non-submasks?
Use the idiom sub = (sub - 1) & m starting from sub = m, stopping after processing sub = 0. It visits every submask once.
Wrap that submask walk inside a loop over all masks m. Summing over all m, the total submask count is 3ⁿ.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Across all masks, the number of (mask, submask) pairs is Σ 2^popcount(m) = 3ⁿ (each bit is independently absent, present-in-both, or present-only-in-m). So O(3ⁿ) time; F is O(2ⁿ) space.
approaches.explanation:
Compute each F[m] independently by visiting only the submasks of m.

**The submask idiom.** Given a mask `m`, the loop `sub = m; sub = (sub - 1) & m` enumerates every submask in strictly decreasing order, ending at 0. The `& m` step keeps you inside m's bits; subtracting 1 borrows through the lowest set bit just like ordinary binary counting confined to the mask.

**Accumulate.** For each `m`, sum `A[sub]` over all its submasks into `F[m]`. Handle `sub = 0` explicitly so the loop terminates after processing the empty submask.

**Why the cost is 3ⁿ, not 4ⁿ.** For each of the n bits, a (mask, submask) pair is in one of three states: the bit is in neither, in the mask only, or in both. That's `3` choices per bit, hence `3ⁿ` total pairs — the exact number of submask visits.

**Why we improve it.** 3ⁿ is far worse than 2ⁿ. At n = 20 it's ~3.5 billion versus the SOS DP's ~21 million. The naive version re-derives shared sub-sums for many masks; SOS DP shares them.
approaches.insight: The submask idiom `(sub - 1) & m` is the canonical way to walk subsets of a mask, but doing it per mask recomputes overlapping work. The leap is realizing those overlaps form a prefix-sum structure along each bit axis.

Add the current submask's value into F[m].
0 is the last submask; break after counting it to avoid an infinite loop.

Forgetting & m, so the walk leaves m's bits and adds wrong entries.

approaches.name: Sum Over Subsets DP — Bit by Bit (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Phrase it as 'a multidimensional prefix sum: relax one bit dimension at a time'.
hints: Picture masks as corners of an n-D cube. A 1-D prefix sum sweeps one axis; how would you prefix-sum along every bit axis in turn?
Process bits one at a time. After handling bit i, F[mask] should equal the sum of A over submasks that agree with mask on bits above i and are ≤ mask on bits 0..i.
For each bit i, for every mask with bit i set, do F[mask] += F[mask ^ (1<<i)]. The cleared-bit entry already holds the partial sum from earlier bits — that's why the loop order matters.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two nested loops: n bits times 2ⁿ masks, with O(1) work each — O(2ⁿ · n). The DP runs in place on F (a copy of A), so space is O(2ⁿ).
approaches.explanation:
Treat the subset sum as a prefix sum performed independently along each of the n bit dimensions.

**The hypercube view.** Index masks as 0/1 vectors of length n — the corners of an n-dimensional cube. F[m] sums A over every corner componentwise ≤ m (every submask). A classic n-dimensional prefix sum computes exactly this if you prefix-sum along one axis at a time; SOS DP is that idea applied to the Boolean cube.

**The per-bit relaxation.** Start with `F = A`. For bit `i` from 0 to n - 1, scan every mask. If `mask` has bit `i` set, add `F[mask ^ (1 << i)]` into `F[mask]`. In words: a mask that includes element `i` absorbs the accumulated value of the otherwise-identical mask that excludes `i`.

**The invariant that makes it correct.** After processing bits `0..i`, `F[mask]` holds the sum of `A[s]` over all submasks `s` that match `mask` exactly on bits `> i` and may differ freely on bits `0..i`. Each new bit `i` extends the freedom by one dimension. After the last bit, `mask` may differ on all bits below it — i.e. `F[mask]` is the sum over all submasks.

**Why the loop order is non-negotiable.** When you process bit `i`, the entry `F[mask ^ (1 << i)]` must already reflect bits `0..i-1` but **not** bit `i`. Because bit `i` is clear in `mask ^ (1 << i)`, this round leaves it untouched, so reading it is safe and adds no double-count. Swapping the loops (masks outside, bits inside) destroys this staging and produces wrong sums.

**Superset variant.** To sum over supersets instead, keep the same skeleton but update the cleared-bit entry from the set-bit one: `F[mask ^ (1 << i)] += F[mask]`. Same O(2ⁿ · n) cost, opposite direction on the lattice.
approaches.insight: SOS DP is the subset-lattice analogue of a 2-D prefix sum done row-sweep then column-sweep. Each bit is an axis; relaxing it once accumulates that axis. Because the axes are independent, n single-axis sweeps compose into the full subset sum — turning 3ⁿ overlapping walks into 2ⁿ · n disjoint updates.

dryRun.intro: F starts as a copy of A = [3,1,4,2]. Relax bit 0, then bit 1.

java.explanation: Each mask starts holding only its own value; the DP grows the sums in place.
Outer loop over bit dimensions — this MUST be the outer loop.
Only masks containing bit i absorb the sub-sum from below this axis.
Add the partial sum of the same mask with bit i cleared; safe because that entry hasn't seen bit i yet.

python.explanation: Copy A so the input stays intact; DP runs in place on F.
Relax one bit dimension per outer iteration.
Update only masks that include element i.
Pull in the accumulated value of the bit-i-cleared mask — the prefix-sum step along axis i.

edgeCases.behavior: Every F[mask] stays 0; sums of zeros.
A[2ⁿ-1]=v has no proper supermask, so only F[2ⁿ-1]=v changes.
~21M updates; use 64-bit accumulators to avoid overflow on large value sums.

pitfalls: Swapping the loop order (masks outside, bits inside) — breaks the per-bit staging invariant.
Updating masks where bit i is clear, or reading F[mask | (1<<i)] — both double-count.
Using 32-bit ints when many values sum into one mask — overflow.

commonMistakes: Nesting the loops as masks-outer, bits-inner, which violates the dimension-by-dimension invariant.
Adding F[mask ^ (1<<i)] for masks where bit i is NOT set, mixing the two halves wrongly.
Accumulating into a 32-bit type and overflowing when many large values combine.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Loop order swapped
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If masks are the outer loop and bits the inner, F[mask ^ (1<<i)] may already include bit i's contribution from a later bit's pass, double-counting and corrupting sums.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong neighbor read
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reading the supermask F[mask | (1<<i)] instead of the cleared-bit submask F[mask ^ (1<<i)] computes a different (and inconsistent) quantity, not the subset sum.
